signals.title: @rajend86: Beyond Earth: Space-Based Computing, Satellite Intelligence and the Future of Orbital Infrastructure Introduction Space infrastructure is en
signals.content: Beyond Earth: Space-Based Computing, Satellite Intelligence and the Future of Orbital Infrastructure Introduction Space infrastructure is entering a new phase of development. Satellites already support communication, navigation, weather forecasting, Earth observation and scientific research. As launch systems, satellite manufacturing and onboard computing continue to advance, space may become an increasingly important part of the global digital infrastructure ecosystem. The next generation of space systems could combine satellite networks, intelligent onboard processing, optical communications, autonomous operations and advanced ground-based computing. More ambitious concepts include orbital data centers and space-based computing platforms. These ideas are attracting attention, but their technical and commercial feasibility remains an important question. The long-term opportunity is to build a connected infrastructure system that extends from Earth into orbit and potentially beyond. 1. The Evolution of Satellite Infrastructure Earlier satellite systems were often designed for specialized communication, navigation or observation tasks. Modern satellite networks increasingly use interconnected constellations. These systems can support: - Broadband connectivity - Earth observation - Environmental monitoring - Disaster response - Maritime tracking - Agricultural intelligence - Remote industrial communications - Scientific research Satellite technology is becoming more closely connected with terrestrial telecommunications and cloud infrastructure. 2. The Emergence of Space-Based Intelligence Earth observation satellites generate enormous quantities of information. Traditional systems frequently transmit collected data to ground stations for processing. However, transmitting every image and measurement can require substantial communication capacity. Onboard processing offers another approach. Satellites can increasingly use specialized processors and AI models to analyze selected information before transmitting results. Potential applications include: - Detecting wildfires - Monitoring floods - Identifying changes in land use - Tracking agricultural conditions - Observing infrastructure - Monitoring maritime activity - Identifying environmental changes This creates the concept of space-based intelligence: processing information closer to where it is collected. 3. AI at the Edge of Space AI systems operating on satellites face different constraints from conventional data-center environments. They must operate within limitations involving: - Electrical power - Heat removal - Radiation exposure - Physical size - Communication availability - Hardware reliability - Maintenance access Space-qualified computing systems must be designed for demanding environmental conditions. Not every commercial GPU or AI accelerator can simply be installed on a satellite. Specialized hardware, software optimization and radiation-tolerant design may be necessary depending on the mission. 4. Optical Communication and Satellite Networks Future space infrastructure may rely increasingly on optical communication. Laser communication systems can provide high-bandwidth links between compatible satellites and ground infrastructure. Potential advantages include high data rates and reduced dependence on some radio-frequency spectrum resources. However, optical communication requires precise pointing, acquisition and tracking. Atmospheric conditions can also affect satellite-to-ground optical links. Radio-frequency systems will remain important, and future networks may combine multiple communication technologies.

Text displayed in the video reads: “Do you think CENTCOM will once again post a ‘fact-check,’ claiming that all U.S. military assets are safe and sound and that none of them have been targeted by the IRGC?!” #IRGC #Iran #IranWar #WestAsia #USA

signals.brief_en: The IRGC released video showing the moment two U.S. drones—an MQ‑9 Reaper and an MQ‑1 Predator—were reportedly shot down over the Strait of Hormuz. The on‑screen caption questions whether CENTCOM will issue a fact‑check claiming all U.S. assets remain safe and un‑targeted. No independent verification of the shoot‑downs is currently available; open‑source imagery and satellite data have not confirmed the loss of the platforms. The claim, if true, would represent a rare successful anti‑air operation by Iran in a heavily monitored maritime chokepoint, potentially affecting U.S. ISR posture and regional deterrence calculations. Analysts should monitor further OSINT corroboration, including radar tracks, loss reports, and statements from U.S. Central Command.

signals.title: @DavidLinthicum: The Global Outage Mea Culpa: Why Enterprise Cloud Trust Is Officially Broken A stage apology and an admission of having work to do do not qu
signals.content: The Global Outage Mea Culpa: Why Enterprise Cloud Trust Is Officially Broken A stage apology and an admission of having work to do do not qualify as an explanation, especially not when global commerce just took a direct hit. Satya Nadella addressed last week's catastrophic Outlook blackout at Ignite by framing digital infrastructure as the dial tone for the world, before quickly steering the conversation right back to Copilot and the next cycle of product announcements. https://t.co/tTVRmouzM3 The enterprise cannot simply shrug this off and proceed as normal. Over the past week, I have been talking directly with enterprise leaders whose critical operations ground to a complete standstill. Across my client base alone, the financial fallout from operational paralysis, stranded transactions, and lost productivity easily exceeds 1 billion USD. For these organizations, trust has evaporated. They are no longer having hypothetical strategy sessions; they are actively discussing an exodus from their Microsoft infrastructure to protect their businesses from catastrophic vendor concentration risk. From an engineering perspective, there is zero excuse for this failure mode. You do not design and operate a tier-one global cloud architecture where a single deployment mistake or routing flaw can propagate unrestricted across international boundaries and knock out services in dozens of countries simultaneously. Fundamental distributed systems architecture requires rigid blast-radius containment, decoupled fault domains, and autonomous regional isolation. If an operational issue can still cascade globally through automated traffic management and bring down key gateway tiers worldwide, it points to systemic failure. Either the underlying architecture is abysmal, the operational and deployment controls are fundamentally broken, or critical resiliency engineering has been ignored while chasing feature releases. Brushing off a worldwide blackout as an unfortunate mistake while pivoting straight into sales mode is unacceptable for an infrastructure provider. Until leadership provides a comprehensive, transparent architectural accounting of why isolation failed at a planetary scale, every CIO and enterprise architect should treat their single-vendor exposure as an active operational liability. #CloudComputing #EnterpriseArchitecture #CloudReliability #Microsoft365 #CIO #TechStrategy #DisasterRecovery

signals.brief_en: The recent Outlook outage, highlighted by Satya Nadella at Ignite, exposed a critical failure in Microsoft’s global cloud architecture. Enterprise customers experienced complete service loss, resulting in over $1 billion in estimated financial damage and a rapid erosion of trust. Leaders are now evaluating migration away from Microsoft to mitigate vendor concentration risk. The incident underscores the need for stricter blast‑radius containment, robust change‑control, and transparent incident communication in tier‑one cloud services.
